entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
Students read Norse mythology for a term, enjoy a term of fairy tales from around the world collected or written in the 19th century, and finish with a term of African American folktales.

This topic is included in the following course(s): Literature: Grade 4

About Literature: Grade 4
Overview note: Literature selections are chosen to encourage students to engage with rich ideas in literature and history and also to help them to gain independence in their reading and lessons.

Mythology/Hist. Fiction: Grade 4
In the Days of Giants tells the stories of Norse mythology and is read in Terms 1-2. The Nordic people would enjoy telling tales of heroes, gods, and monsters during the long, dark winter nights. As such, we recommend teachers preview the readings to ensure they are suitable for their particular students.

Term 2 (Folk Tales): Older Folk Tales often include content such as drinking, smoking, abuse of others, etc. The teacher should preview the tales if this might be an issue for your home or classroom.

blocks.text:
• Read through the lesson and gather any materials or find any necessary links. 

• If you have not already read the book, you may want to read the selected pages in advance, especially for Shakespeare lessons. It is helpful to read the play or a preview of it beforehand.

• Choose which books to have students start reading independently (General Literature selections are especially good for independent work).

• Connect back to the previous lesson. Ask students to give a summary of what they remember and/or predict what might come next. (Full narration is not necessary.)

• If students have difficulty recalling, teachers might try showing them an illustration, sharing something that the teacher remembers, or prompting them with the first sentence of the last reading. This will often refresh their memory enough to allow them to recall.

• If students still cannot recall anything from the last reading, then teachers might consider continuing anyway (with a shorter reading and/or using a combination of visual and audio support this time) or repeating the last lesson, depending on the reading and the nature of the book.

• Use a picture, map, or engaging question to pique the student's interest in the day's lesson. 

• If necessary, you may talk about one or two unfamiliar words that will be crucial to understanding.

• Read the day's passage aloud or have students read independently. For Shakespeare, it is highly recommended that each student have their own copy of the play and that you read it aloud together or read along and underline/make notes while listening to the audio recording.

• Use supportive strategies and educational tools to reduce frustration and better engage the mind, as appropriate. These could include, but are not limited to, the use of eBooks, pictures, audio, read-aloud, buddy reading, colored reading strips, etc.

• Some students may benefit from having a notebook or piece of scrap paper available to externalize ideas by drawing, recording names, or making symbolic 'squiggle' notes.

• Students who have a difficult time sitting still or listening may benefit from: a fidget of their choice, such as a piece of putty or clay or an afghan; flexible positioning, such as a wobble seat or inverted sitting; or sensory modulation, such as a weighted vest or blanket or adjustment of light, temperature, or sound.

• Have students retell the passage orally or in writing. If writing, encourage students to use the full remaining lesson time and include as much detail as they can remember. For Shakespeare or challenging books, it may be helpful to narrate more frequently and/or use props.

• Alternatively, learners may use words, pictures, Legos, dolls, etc., to process and convey ideas in the manner most natural to them.  

• Students who used paper or a notebook to externalize may refer to these for support. Other students who need external support may benefit from looking at a map or picture from the book while narrating.

• Students who tend to use the same type of narration all the time might be encouraged to try another form of narration by first doing it together through play or discussion.

• Teachers may take turns to model.

• Narration is a complex skill that requires coordination of several parts of the brain. If a student struggles to narrate in general, with a specific subject or book, or on one day but not others, then this is an opportunity to learn. Observe when they struggle with this or any other activity today; notice facial expressions and body language; listen to what they say about why it is hard or how they feel about it. Take note of these observations for later, tell them that you see how hard they are working, and then offer whatever support they need to end on a positive note or take a break for the day, if necessary.

• Give the student an opportunity to share thoughts on the lesson and any connections made.  

• To stimulate discussion, you can ask an open-ended question or use an included discussion question.

lessons.title: 20m Mythology/Hist. Fiction: Grade 4 - Lesson 17
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: South American Jungle Tales 

➜ INTRO
For centuries, people shared stories out loud around fires, at celebrations, and before bed. By the 1800s, many people worried these beloved tales were disappearing as the world rapidly changed around them, so collectors began writing them down. The Brothers Grimm gathered folk tales across Germany, Hans Christian Andersen turned Danish traditions into fairy tales, and Andrew Lang collected stories from countries all over the world. In America, people began recording the stories of Indigenous communities and formerly enslaved people. Now it's your turn to explore these timeless tales and discover the stories people have treasured for generations. We'll start our journey in South America with a tale about a lazy bee. 

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
"The Lazy Bee" Read from the beginning to "inside a hollow tree."   

• What do you think will happen next? 

➜ MAP WORK
Find the continent of South America on a map or globe. Our first tale takes place in the country of Argentina. See if you can find Argentina on your map. (The story mentioned the city of Misiones. Misiones is actually not a city, but is one of the provinces of Argentina.)
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER NOTE
The world of folk tales is vast. Explore extra helpings for other tales to include or substitute as desired. For instance, Favorite African Folk Tales by Nelson Mandela features many short tales that could easily be added to a lesson or enjoyed as a read-aloud. 

Note that a Christmas tale is in the final two lessons of the term. Feel free to swap around the order of the tales if needed to read that story closer to Christmas.

lessons.title: 20m Mythology/Hist. Fiction: Grade 4 - Lesson 20
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Russian Fairy Tales 

➜ INTRO
Our next tales come from Russia. Russia is a vast land with a rich culture full of art, music, poetry, and storytelling stretching back hundreds of years. Its folk tales offer a window into a culture that loved nature, prized humility, and understood that life held both joy and hardship. Heroes in these stories are often humble and kind rather than powerful and proud, and magic is woven naturally into the everyday world. As you read, remember that you are not just enjoying a good story, but catching a glimpse of a way of life.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
Tsar Sultan: Read from the beginning to "written in a tale."

• Does this fairy tale remind you of any others you have heard? 

➜ MAPWORK
Find Russia on a map. The land occupied by Russia has changed over many years. In the 1800's, Russia even owned the land that is now the state of Alaska. Russia sold Alaska to the United States in 1867, though it didn't become a state until almost 100 years later, in 1959.

lessons.title: 20m Mythology/Hist. Fiction: Grade 4 - Lesson 22
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: "Papa's Christmas Story" (aka A Scot's Christmas Story) by George MacDonald

➜ INTRO
George MacDonald was a Scottish storyteller (1823-1905). He loved fairy tales and fantasy, and even inspired C.S. Lewis, who wrote The Chronicles of Narnia! MacDonald was a devoted Christian, and his faith showed in his writing. He loved Christmas so much that he would carol through the streets with his children and sometimes invite over a hundred strangers into his home to celebrate! He wrote Christmas poems, songs, and stories to share that joy with others. Today you're going to read one of his Christmas stories called "Papa's Story" (sometimes called "A Scot's Christmas"). In it, a father tells his children a tale on Christmas Eve. As you read, think about what lessons might be hiding inside, just like the other tales we have read. 

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
"Papa's Christmas Story" (aka A Scot's Christmas Story) by George MacDonald 
p.40-48 til "He soon fell asleep."
∞ Link: "Papa's Christmas Story

• What do you think Nelly has made up her mind to do? 

➜ MAPWORK (optional)
This tale takes place in Scotland. Find Scotland on a map or globe.

lessons.title: 20m Mythology/Hist. Fiction: Grade 4 - Lesson 25
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Tales of Uncle Remus

PREP: For history and context on this collection of Brer Rabbit tales and their broader relevance, read Julius Lester's Foreword on p.xiii-xxi.

➜ INTRO
Many different stories were published and told in the 1700s. Some stories that became increasingly popular were about a rabbit. A rabbit is the main character in many folktales from Africa, and as more and more people in Africa were enslaved and brought to the American colonies, "...they took stories from home about a hare – Wakaima – and adapted them to their new surroundings" (viii). Over time, a new set of stories developed about a rabbit, now named Brer Rabbit, through this interaction of cultures from Africa, America, and the West Indies. The stories were told aloud and changed depending on the storyteller and the listener, so while they are old stories, they are also new every time they are told.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.4-10 "How Brer Fox and Brer Dog Became Enemies," “Hold’im Down, Brer Fox," "Brer Rabbit Comes to Dinner"
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER NOTE
There is an audiobook version of these tales read by the author, which is a great option to give students a bit more independence and allow them to experience the stories orally. Note that only selections of the book are included in the lesson plans. Some of the omitted stories have content you might want to preview before allowing students to listen to the whole book.

terms.content: · In the Days of Giants: Give a short account of one of Odin's or Loki's adventures using words or pictures.

· Tell about a favorite fairy or folk tale you read this term and what lesson or moral the tale was trying to share.

· Why do tales from different countries and cultures have things in common with each other? Give some examples of similar tales.
· Tales of Uncle Remus: Tell the story of Brer Rabbit and Brer Turtle OR tell a story about Brer Rabbit and Brer Fox.
